paras: Verdana Foods is a mid-sized food manufacturer in Curitiba with four plants and one finance team. In 2024 the team closed the month in nine days. Invoices from suppliers arrived by email, somebody typed them into SAP, and a second person checked every line.

Verdana chose Invent in January 2025. The team did not replace SAP. They connected it to the supplier portal and to their bank, and they ran a pilot in one plant for six weeks before they rolled it out to the other three.

The pilot was not smooth. In the second week the bank changed its file format, and the nightly sync failed for three days. Our team found the problem, fixed it, and wrote the fix into the product, so it has not happened again, at Verdana or anywhere else.

Since then the numbers have changed. The close has dropped from nine days to four, and invoice turnaround time has fallen from three days to one. Adoption has reached ninety per cent of the finance team, and nobody has typed an invoice by hand since July. The project has already paid for itself.
Verdana has asked us to add two more plants this year, and their finance director has agreed to take reference calls from other customers. She has done four so far.

tips: A finished date means past simple.

A result that is true now, with no finished time: present perfect.

For plus a period, still true today: present perfect.

When asks for a finished time, so the answer is past simple.

Since plus a starting point takes the present perfect.

listenings.text: I have written about two hundred case studies, and most of the ones that failed made the same mistake. They started with the product. Nobody cares about the product in the first paragraph. They care about the customer, and they care about one number: where the customer was before anything changed. That is the baseline, and without it every result is just an adjective. Faster than what? Cheaper than when? So the order I use is always the same. First, the situation, in the past, with a date. Then what the customer decided, and what happened, also in the past. And only then the results, in the present, because the results are still true today. The close has dropped to four days. Adoption has reached ninety per cent. If the numbers are still true, say them as if they are still true. And one more thing. Put in the part that went wrong. Buyers do not believe stories where nothing went wrong.

When a vendor sends me a case study, I read it in about forty seconds, and I am looking for three things. The first is a name I can call. A logo on a slide is not a reference. A finance director who has agreed to take my call is a reference. The second is a baseline with a date on it, because an improvement of sixty per cent means nothing if I do not know what it was sixty per cent of. And the third is the problem. Every implementation I have ever seen has had a bad week, and when a case study has no bad week in it, I assume somebody has removed it. So the case studies that actually move me are the honest ones. Here is what went wrong, here is when it happened, here is how quickly it was fixed, and here is what has changed since. That last sentence is the one I remember.
